title: Rohatsu again
hookLine: the week of sitting for the awakening

lines: THE LAST NIGHT OF THE WEEK.
ONE BRIGHT POINT IN THE EAST.
cards: The last night of the week. In a cold Zen hall, nobody has lain down. The candles are low.
Legs ache. Someone's stomach growls, loud, and nobody laughs. Then the windows begin to gray, and low in the east, before the sun, one bright point of light hangs over the trees.
In Zen tellings, that's the moment: the seeker under the tree looks up at the morning star and wakes. Rohatsu is the week of sitting that ends there.
You've stayed through the last night before, and the middle of the week with Mara's army. This year, listen for what tradition says came out of his mouth when it was over.

teach.b: First, the verses. The Dhammapada holds two short verses that the commentary tradition places on the Buddha's lips at the moment of awakening.
He speaks to a builder: the one who keeps putting up the house of a self, life after life. He says he went looking for that builder through many births, and birth again and again was painful.
Then the turn, in Max Müller's words: "But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again."
Tabernacle is an old word for a tent or a house. The verse goes on to say the rafters are broken and the ridge-pole shattered. Who is the builder?
The commentary reads it as the mind's own craving, the thirst that keeps reaching and keeps making a shelter out of me and mine. It was never an enemy outside.
It was a habit, and once it was seen clearly, it couldn't keep building. So why a week of sitting? The house isn't taken down by force.

It's seen. And seeing needs stillness, so for a week, from before dawn into the night, people in Zen halls sit and watch the builder at work: the plans, the worries, the little stories of who they are.
This week on the path walked the festival year: the wheel set rolling, the rains, the ancestors, the invitation, the gifts, the descent.
It ends where the teaching began: one person, sitting still until the morning star.

how: In Zen monasteries in Japan and elsewhere, monks and lay practitioners sit an intensive week-long retreat called Rohatsu sesshin, ending on the day kept for the Buddha's awakening, sometimes sitting through the final night.

o: a Zen new year's feast held at the winter solstice
the Zen week of sitting that ends on the awakening's day
a night vigil for the Buddha's death, kept in Japan

p: craving, making a house of a self
an old word for a tent or house
seen at the awakening, in Zen tellings

s: the house-builder in the verses is an enemy outside the mind
in the commentary's reading, the builder is the mind's own craving, seen clearly and stopped.
the commentary tradition places these verses at the moment of awakening
they're kept in the Dhammapada as words spoken when he woke.
in the verse, the house is torn down by force
the builder has been seen. once seen, it can't keep building.

games.q: it's the last night of Rohatsu. a worry about tomorrow starts building in your mind, plank by plank. what does today's practice suggest?
o: notice the builder at work, let it go, and return to the breath.
get up and deal with tomorrow now.
games.why: the verse doesn't smash the house. the builder is seen, and that is enough to stop the building.

practice: Sit as still as is comfortable and watch for the builder: a plan for later, a worry about someone, a story about yourself.
Don't fight it; just notice, there's the builder picking up a plank, and come back to the breath, again and again.
When the bell rings, stay a little longer if you can, the way the Zen halls sit through the night; even one more breath counts.

wordCard.voice: Rohatsu. The Zen week of sitting that ends on the day kept for the awakening, when tradition says the Buddha saw the morning star. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali gahakaraka: house-builder, the one the Buddha addresses in Dhammapada 153–154.

carryVoice: Your line: the morning star. One bright point before sunrise, and a builder seen. A week of festivals, done.
